Proteas at the Cricket World Cup

By: Julian Sun | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We look back at the South Africa's history at the Cricket World Cup

Unique Selling Point:
For the majority of South Africans, winning the Cricket World Cup remains the Holy Grail for the Proteas. Since participating in their first world cup back in 1992, the team has come so close, yet remained so far from attaining this treasured goal. We look back at the highlights and heartbreaks over the course of 7 previous campaigns as they embark on their latest campaign at the 2019 Cricket World Cup in England in hopes of breaking a 27-year drought and claim their maiden World Cup.

Summary:
South African cricket had been isolated from the world because of Apartheid for a period of 22 years. Then with the release of Nelson Mandela, South African Cricket was welcomed back into the fold and (at the last minute) invited to participate in the 1992 Cricket World Cup in Australia. So began South Africa's quest to capture the greatest prize in cricket and over the next 27 years, the team would scale the highest of highs and plumb the lowest of lows in trying to bring the cup home.

In this episode of Carte Blanche we look back at the Proteas' history at the Cricket World Cup, reliving the moments of triumph and the depths of despair through the eyes of the players that were there.

From beating Australia in their very first game, Jonty Rhodes' announcing himself spectacularly on the world stage, to rain denying South Africa a place in the final to Lance Kluseners' remarkable exploits at the 1999 World Cup to the epic semi-final against Australia or most recently, South Africa's painful exit against New Zealand in the last World Cup, South Africa's relationship with the World Cup has always been fraught with drama.

We will speak to Proteas' legends like Gary Kirsten, Lance Klusener, Shaun Pollock, Herschelle Gibbs, Makhaya Ntini & Graeme Smith to interrogate what makes the World Cup so special and why winning it remains the Holy Grail for South African Cricket.

Press Release:


The Curse of the Chokers
So near and yet so far – that’s the curse that’s haunted the South Africa’s National cricket team at every World Cup for the last twenty seven years. Aptly nicknamed “Chokers”, winning the tournament remains the Holy Grail and wholly unattainable dream for the Proteas. Gary Kirsten, Lance Klusener and Makhaya Ntini are some of the giants of South African cricket who have stood on the battlefield – and lost. Now only days before this year’s contest, Carte Blanche relives the moments of triumph and the depths of despair and asks whether the new crop of players can rewrite history.
Producer: Julian Sun
Presenter: Macfarlane Moleli


Script:


V/O: The Cricket World Cup is one of the biggest sporting spectacles on the planet, comparable to the Olympic Games and the FIFA World Cup in popularity.

Since its inception in 1975, there have been 11 editions of the Cricket World Cup and the last one held in 2015, saw an estimated viewing audience of 2.2 billion people.

Macfarlane: After decades in isolation, South African cricket played its maiden cricket world cup way back in 1992. Since then the Proteas have endured 27 years of heartbreak and near misses in an ongoing quest for cricket’s holy grail.
V/O: Neil Manthorp is a journalist whose followed all of South Africa’s World Cup exploits.

Neil Manthorp comment


In the twilight of his career, Peter Kirsten believed he’d never play international cricket but the release Nelson Mandela changed everything…

Comments about SA v Aus

V/O: What they lacked in experience, they made up for in exuberance, led by the fielding exploits of a young Jonty Rhodes who announced himself to the world with one of the most breath-taking moments in World Cup history.

Comments about Jonty runout

V/O: South Africa surprised the world by making it to a semi-final against England.

They were looking on track for victory when rain cruelly intervened.

SA V Eng Semi Final 22 runs off 1 ball


V/O: It was heartbreak for South Africa… the first of many.


V/O: The Proteas arrived at the 1999 World Cup in England as the number 1 ranked team in the world.

Neil Manthorp on the 1999 team

V/O: The man of the tournament was Lance Klusener

Lance Klusener comment

V/O: The team looked unstoppable when they took to the field for a mouth-watering semi-final against Australia

Regarded as the best game in World Cup history, this epic encounter saw the Proteas looking down and out before Lance Klusener’s heroics brought them back in to the match.

With the scores tied and just one run required off the last 4 balls, victory looked assured. Then a moment of madness that remains seared into the very soul of South African cricket.

SA v Australia 1999
V/O: 4 years later at the 2003 World Cup held in South Africa, The Proteas looked to lay to rest the ghosts of that semi final tie.

Eric Simons was the coach then. Being the host nation came with unique pressure.

Eric Simons on Pressure






Losses against West Indies and New Zealand in the group stages led to a must-win game against Sri Lanka in Durban.

The equation was simple: win and progress to the knock-out stages, Lose and go home.

However what wasn’t simple was Duckworth Lewis, a method for calculating run rate during rain interrupted matches.

Eric & Neil on SA failing to read Duckworth Lewis properly.


V/O: The loss was devastating. This catalogue of disappointment has resulted in the label of “chokers”, a burden that grows heavier with each World Cup failure.

Comments about choking

At the 2015 World Cup, a win against Sri Lanka in the quarters set up a semi-final clash against New Zealand, where the Proteas dared to dream once more.

but once again, another epic match ended in crushing defeat

SA vs NZ 2015



V/O: And so to the 2019 World Cup in England starting next week.

For the first time since their debut, The Proteas arrive not as favourites but as genuine underdogs.

Comments about the 2019 squad

V/O: So can the squad of 2019 comprising of youngsters playing their first world cup (like KG Rabada) and veterans playing their last (like Hashim Amla) finally cross the threshold and win the World Cup?
